title: Outreach Emails QA Report
summary: QA report on 3 Piece Special outreach emails cross-checked against work.md.
content:
Elmer QA Report -- Outreach Emails (3 Piece Special)

Date: 2026-03-09 Reviewed: jacob-session.md, jacob-mar11-batch.md, jacob-mar12-batch.md, jacob-mar13-batch.md Cross-checked: alex-outreach-review.md, context/work.md

Alex Review: Agreement and Pushback

Where Alex is right (amplified)

1. Included Health language is misleading. This is the biggest issue in the entire outreach.

Alex nailed this. "We've been working with Included Health on video content" implies an ongoing relationship. It's a $9k one-off event shoot that hasn't even happened yet as of today (Mar 9 is day 1 of the 3-day summit). So as of drafting, AOM had not yet produced anything for Included Health. The emails are written in past tense about work that is currently in progress or hasn't started.

This isn't just a tone issue. If a prospect replies and asks to see the Included Health work, there's nothing to show. That's a credibility problem. Alex was right to flag it but actually undersold the severity.

Jacob: Fix every Included Health reference. Options:

  • If these go out after Mar 11 (summit wraps): "We just produced a 3-day video shoot for Included Health" is accurate.
  • If these go out before the summit wraps: Drop the Included Health name entirely. Use Virtu Hospitality (which is on the website) or go proof-point-free on healthcare emails and lead purely on the pain point.
  • Never say "we've been working with" or "we've been doing video for." That language implies ongoing retainer work. It's not true.

2. Subject lines are a real problem.

Alex is correct that "quick question for [Company]" is generic and especially weak for:

  • Mar 11 batch: These prospects already saw this exact subject line ~330 days ago and didn't reply. Sending the same format again is asking to be ignored.
  • Mar 12/13 batches: These are cold first-touch. "Quick question" gives no signal about who AOM is or why the email matters. It reads like SaaS sales automation.

3. The Ambition Mechanical proof point is undersold.

Alex is right. The emails say "a Phoenix HVAC company" or "a Phoenix contractor" when the website literally names Ambition Mechanical with stats, photos, and a link. The vague version reads like AOM is hiding something. The specific version reads like AOM has real work to show.

4. AI differentiator is missing.

Agree with Alex. Not a single email across 50+ drafts mentions AI, automation, or the content system. This is the one thing that separates AOM from every other "we do video for contractors" agency. It doesn't need to be the lead, but zero mentions is a miss.

Where Alex is wrong or overcorrecting

1. Adding pricing to the website is not Jacob's problem to solve.

Alex recommends adding "$3k/month" language to the website to match what the emails imply. That's a website/strategy decision, not an outreach fix. Jacob shouldn't be adjusting email copy to match a website that might change next week. The emails should be accurate to what AOM actually offers. If AOM offers a $3k retainer (it does, per work.md), the emails can reference it. The website catching up is Bobby's job.

2. The "steal the website headline" suggestion is surface-level.

Alex says the website headline ("WE MAKE COMPANIES IMPOSSIBLE TO IGNORE") is better than any email subject line. That's true in isolation, but putting a brand tagline as a cold email subject line will get filtered or ignored. It reads like marketing copy, not a person writing an email. The subject line needs to feel like a human sent it, not a campaign.

Alex's alternative suggestions ("your competitors are getting better at content," "one filming day, one month of posts") are better than the tagline but still need testing. I'd add:

  • "content for [trade]" (simple, specific, not clever)
  • "[Company] + video" (direct, scannable)
  • "saw your work" (for construction companies with visible project portfolios)

3. Alex's revised proof section is too long for a cold email.

Alex suggests: "We just built the full digital presence for Ambition Mechanical, a Phoenix HVAC company: website, monthly filming, and a content system that produces 30+ posts a month. What moved the needle was showing the crew and the work, not stock photos. You can see it at ambitionac.com."

That's 45 words for just the proof section. In a 75-word email, that leaves 30 words for everything else. The fix is right (name Ambition, add the URL), but the execution needs to be tighter:

"We just built the full brand presence for Ambition Mechanical, a Phoenix HVAC company -- 30+ posts/month, website, monthly filming. Take a look: ambitionac.com"

That's 26 words. Same info, half the space.

4. Alex missed the Feb 28 check-in batch severity.

Alex calls them "dead weight" and says don't send a second round. Correct. But he doesn't flag that 35 of these 37 are STILL SITTING AS DRAFTS in Gmail, unsent. They were never sent. The Mar 10 session log confirms this. So the question isn't whether to follow up on the Feb 28 batch. It's whether to send the original Feb 28 batch at all. And the answer is: no, not in this format. One-liner bumps with no personalization, no proof point, and no value prop will get zero replies. They should be rewritten or abandoned.

Independent Email QA

Feb 28 Apollo Batch (37 check-ins in jacob-session.md)

Rating: REWRITE

Every single email is identical: "Hi [First name], just wanted to bump this up in case it got buried. Happy to hop on a quick call if the timing's right."

Problems:

  • Zero personalization. No mention of what the original email was about.
  • No value. Nothing new is being offered.
  • "In case it got buried" is a guilt-trip opener. It sounds passive-aggressive.
  • No proof point, no CTA beyond "hop on a quick call."
  • Sending this to 37 people on the same day from the same email will trigger spam filters.
  • 35 of 37 haven't even been sent yet. Don't send them as-is.

Jacob: If any of these 37 are worth re-engaging, write them a real email with a niche angle, a proof point, and a reason to reply. Batch them in groups of 5-8, not 37 at once. If they're not worth a custom email, they're not worth emailing.

Elijah Salazar (Email 1 in jacob-session.md)

Rating: PASS

Good email. Correctly references the prior conversation. Specific to the context (paid ads video, YouTube content). Clear CTA. Doesn't over-explain. Only note: "things have settled a bit" is filler. Cut it.

Line edit:

  • Change: "I wanted to circle back now that things have settled a bit."
  • To: "Wanted to circle back."

Paige Soucie (Email 2 in jacob-session.md)

Rating: PASS

Warm, appropriate for the relationship. Doesn't push. Keeps the door open. Nothing to fix.

Mar 11 Batch -- Tier 1 Re-engagement (19 emails)

Rating: NEEDS REVISION

The per-company niche angles are genuinely good. Jacob did real research. The healthcare emails identify real pain points (home health visual storytelling, tribal health, brand-name positioning). The real estate emails find specific angles per company type (dual-service, team-based, owner-operator, RE school). This is not cookie-cutter work and it shows.

Issues to fix:

1. Subject lines must change. Every email uses "quick question for [Company]." These prospects saw this exact format 330+ days ago. New subject line, no exceptions.

Recommendations by vertical:

  • Healthcare: "video for [Company]" or "home health content"
  • Real estate: "[Company] + content" or "video for [niche]"

2. Included Health references (Emails 1-5, 10) -- all need the fix described above. "We've been working with" and "We've been doing video for" are inaccurate. Rewrite to reflect actual scope.

3. Real estate emails are missing a proof point. Healthcare emails reference Included Health (even if inaccurately). Real estate emails reference "a Phoenix-area company" vaguely. Name Ambition Mechanical or don't reference it at all. The vague version sounds like you're making it up.

4. Email 2 (Deanna Jackson, Gila River) -- she's an EA to the CEO, not the decision-maker. Jacob flagged this correctly. The email is fine as a routing intro but the CTA should reflect that. Instead of "Are you already working with someone on video or social?" try "Would this be worth forwarding to the right person on your team?"

5. Email 5 (Mattie Gaffney, Abloom) -- the name-based opener is a stretch. "The name Abloom says something -- growth, care, a living thing" reads like the email was written by someone who Googled the company and had nothing else to say. The rest of the email is good. Cut the name analysis and lead with the pain point.

Line edit for Email 5:

  • Cut: "The name Abloom says something -- growth, care, a living thing. That kind of brand identity is rare in home health, and it's the kind of thing that can actually carry content instead of fighting against it."
  • Replace: "Home health brands that have a clear identity tend to punch above their weight on content -- the story is already there, it just needs to be told well."

6. The "Are you already working with someone on video or social?" CTA appears in every single email. It's fine as a CTA, but the repetition across 19 emails means if any two prospects at the same company compare notes, or if anyone forwards multiple emails, it looks templated. Vary the CTA language across the batch. Options:

  • "Are you already working with someone on this?"
  • "Curious if this is on your radar."
  • "Would it be worth a 10-minute call?"
  • "Happy to share what that's looked like if it's relevant."

Some of these already appear as secondary lines. Promote them to primary CTA position for variety.

Mar 12 Batch -- Tier 2 ICP First-Touch (17 emails)

Rating: NEEDS REVISION

Strongest batch of the three. The construction emails are legitimately good. The niche angles are specific and earned: insulation as "invisible work," crane rental as visual spectacle, dental construction as specialist storytelling. These read like someone who actually understands the trade, not like generic outreach.

Issues to fix:

1. Subject lines. Same problem. "Quick question for [Company]" on a cold first-touch where the prospect has zero context. For construction, test: "content for [trade]" or "[Company] + AOM."

2. Included Health references in healthcare emails (13-17) -- same fix as above. Every single healthcare email references Included Health. Same inaccuracy, same risk.

3. Email 12 (Aaron Couste, Superior HVAC) names Ambition Mechanical directly. This is the strongest email in the entire outreach pipeline. It's specific, it's in the same trade, it names the client, and it references what worked. This should be the template for all HVAC and close-adjacent trades, not the exception. BUT: confirm with Patrik that Ambition is approved for name-drop in outreach. The website already publishes it, so this should be a yes, but verify.

4. Email 6 (Andrew Flanagan, Image Building Systems) -- he's a Senior PM/Estimator, not a decision-maker. The email is written as if addressing the company's marketing direction, but a PM/Estimator doesn't own that. Either adjust the angle to speak to his world (project documentation, proposals, RFQ visuals) or flag as a lower-priority send.

5. Email 8 (Troy Black, Crane Rental) -- Sales/Estimator, not owner. Same issue as #4. Jacob flagged this correctly. The email angle is strong but may land with someone who can't act on it. Send at Patrik's discretion.

6. Email 9 (Dana Mifflin, Blue Square Manufacturing) -- "manufacturing content doesn't get made often because it's hard to shoot well." This is true and it's a good line. But then: "We've been doing that for Phoenix-area companies" -- doing what? Making manufacturing content? Name one. If you can't name one, say "We've been doing process-driven video for Phoenix-area companies" which is true (Ambition has process documentation). Don't imply manufacturing-specific experience you don't have.

Line edit for Email 9:

  • Change: "We've been doing that for Phoenix-area companies"
  • To: "We've been producing process-driven video for Phoenix-area companies"

Mar 13 Batch -- Tier 2 ICP Continued (15 emails)

Rating: NEEDS REVISION

Same caliber as Mar 12. Good niche angles. Same structural issues.

Issues to fix:

1. Subject lines. Same fix needed.

2. Included Health references. Same fix needed. Emails 10-15 all reference IH.

3. Email 7 (Lorraine Bergman, Caliente Construction) -- this person already received a check-in email in the Feb 28 batch (jacob-session.md, #28). Sending a new first-touch email to someone who already got the bump will read as either disorganized or automated. Jacob needs to cross-reference the Mar 12/13 batches against the Feb 28 batch and remove duplicates. If Lorraine is worth contacting again, the email needs to reference the prior touch, not pretend it didn't happen.

This is a critical catch. Check the full Mar 12 and Mar 13 batches for any other overlaps with the Feb 28 list. I see the following names that appeared in the Feb 28 Apollo batch and may also appear in later batches:

  • Lorraine Bergman / Caliente Construction (#28 in Feb batch, Email 7 in Mar 13 batch) -- CONFIRMED DUPLICATE

Jacob: Audit all three batches against the Feb 28 list. Any overlap needs to be flagged and the email adjusted or cut.

4. Email 8 (Ed Wenz, MarZee) -- keep it. Jacob's angle is solid. Precision manufacturing is visually compelling and underserved. The ICP adjacency is close enough. Worth the send.

5. Email 9 (Randy Chambers, DSI) -- keep it but temper expectations. Purchasing Manager at a 16-person company will either forward it or ignore it. The email is fine. Just don't count it as a high-probability touch.

6. Email 14 (Joni Condit, La Posada) -- keep if Patrik approves Tucson. The email is well-written and the CCRC angle is specific. The only question is geography. That's Patrik's call.

7. Email 15 (Bryan Madden, YMCA) -- keep. The angle works. Mission-driven storytelling is a real AOM capability (NABI documentary). The YMCA is a recognizable name and the CEO is a real decision-maker. Worth one send.

8. Email 12 (Catherin Vargas, Sunrise Care Homes) -- the email address domain is @azblue.com, not a Sunrise Care Homes domain. This is either a secondary email or the wrong address entirely. Verify before sending. An email about "Sunrise Care Homes" arriving at an @azblue.com address will look wrong.

Batch Ratings Summary

Batch Rating Key Blockers
Feb 28 Apollo (37 check-ins) REWRITE Zero personalization, never sent, spam risk at volume
Elijah Salazar PASS Minor trim needed
Paige Soucie PASS No changes
Mar 11 Tier 1 (19 emails) NEEDS REVISION Subject lines, Included Health accuracy, missing proof points on RE
Mar 12 Tier 2 (17 emails) NEEDS REVISION Subject lines, Included Health accuracy, Lorraine Bergman duplicate check
Mar 13 Tier 2 (15 emails) NEEDS REVISION Subject lines, Included Health accuracy, Catherin Vargas email domain, duplicate audit

Top 5 Fixes Before Anything Goes Out

These are ranked by impact. Fix #1-3 before sending any batch. #4-5 can be addressed per-email.

  1. Fix every Included Health reference. Rewrite to reflect actual scope (one-off 3-day event shoot, not ongoing retainer). If sending before Mar 11, drop the name entirely.

  2. New subject lines for Mar 11/12/13 batches. "Quick question for [Company]" is dead. Use industry-specific or company-specific subjects. Test 2-3 variants.

  3. Audit all batches for duplicates against Feb 28 list. Lorraine Bergman confirmed. Check the rest.

  4. Name Ambition Mechanical in construction emails. Include ambitionac.com as a clickable proof point. Get Patrik's approval on name-dropping in outreach.

  5. Kill or rewrite the Feb 28 batch. 35 unsent one-liner bumps with no personalization. Either write real emails or remove them from the pipeline entirely.

What Alex Missed

  • The Feb 28 drafts were never sent. His review treated them as sent emails with zero replies. They're unsent drafts.
  • Catherin Vargas (@azblue.com) email domain mismatch.
  • Lorraine Bergman duplicate between Feb 28 and Mar 13 batches.
  • The temporal problem with Included Health: as of drafting, the work hadn't happened yet. Alex flagged it as a misrepresentation of scope (one-off vs. ongoing), which is correct, but missed the bigger issue that the work literally didn't exist yet.
  • The CTA repetition across 50+ emails. "Are you already working with someone on video or social?" appears in almost every email. It's fine individually but looks automated at scale.

Bottom Line

Jacob's niche angles are the best part of this outreach. The per-company research is real and it shows. The writing is clean, the tone is right (direct, warm, not salesy), and the emails are the right length.

The problems are structural, not creative: inaccurate proof points, stale subject lines, no deduplication against prior batches, and over-reliance on a single Included Health reference that doesn't hold up to scrutiny.

Fix the five items above and these batches are ready to send. The bones are good.
